title: SEC v. Chenery Corp. (Chenery II)
lead: After its first rationale fails in court, the SEC again denies management the new shares it seeks and explains why the purchases threaten a fair reorganization.

actors.name: Securities and Exchange Commission
actors.role: Agency administering utility holding-company reorganizations and defending its renewed order.

actors.name: Federal Water Service management interests
actors.role: Officers, directors, and controlling shareholders who bought preferred stock during reorganization.

actors.name: Federal Water and Gas Corporation
actors.role: Surviving reorganized company that applied to amend the plan after the first remand.

proceedings: Chenery I set aside the original agency rationale and returned the matter to the SEC.
The SEC denied a post-remand amendment on a newly explained statutory rationale.
The Court of Appeals reversed, reading Chenery I to foreclose that result.
The Supreme Court reversed and sustained the renewed order.
limits: The original report and assigned excerpt give February 8, 1945 for the renewed order; Justia’s reproduction gives February 7. The account preserves this discrepancy and the differing payment descriptions. No general power to issue retroactive legislative rules is inferred.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Management buys preferred shares while its company reorganizes
sections.cue: Why did these purchases affect both value and control?
paragraphs: As successive reorganization plans for Federal Water Service Corporation came before the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) under the Public Utility Holding Company Act of 1935, its officers, directors, and controlling shareholders bought preferred stock on the open market. The fourth plan would convert preferred stock into common shares in the reorganized enterprise. Management’s purchases would thereby produce more than ten percent of the new common stock, and management acknowledged wanting to protect its position in the new company.

The transactions involved neither fraud nor inadequate disclosure. That qualification matters throughout the dispute: the SEC eventually relied on structural conflicts of interest rather than discovering dishonest purchases. In the first proceeding it required public holders and management to receive different treatment. Public holders could obtain new equity, while management would recover acquisition cost with an additional payment instead of the full appreciation and control associated with conversion. The Court’s introductory history describes accumulated dividends; Jackson’s later dissent describes the operative recovery as cost plus four-percent interest. Those different accounts should not be merged into a claim that management received full reorganization value.

sections.title: Chenery I rejects the first explanation and sends the decision back
sections.cue: What was left open for the SEC to decide?
paragraphs: In Chenery I, 318 U.S. 80, the Supreme Court held that the judicial equity principles the SEC had invoked could not sustain its original order. The Court directed further agency proceedings without deciding whether a properly exercised statutory administrative judgment could justify the same treatment.

On remand, the surviving company, Federal Water and Gas Corporation, applied to amend the plan to distribute new common shares to management on the basis of the old preferred holdings. The individual management interests intervened in support. Their immediate objective was parity with public preferred holders in the new company’s equity and voting power.

The SEC denied the application again. This time it expressly relied on the Act’s standards governing fairness, investor protection, and allocation of voting power. The original U.S. Reports scan and assigned excerpt identify the order as February 8, 1945, Release No. 5584; the Justia reproduction prints February 7. The reviewed source preserves that reproduction discrepancy rather than independently settling the underlying order’s date.

The Court of Appeals, 154 F.2d 6, reversed because it understood the first Supreme Court decision to foreclose the renewed refusal. The Supreme Court granted review of this new agency determination. Counsel had not merely supplied an alternative argument for an unchanged agency decision: the Commission itself had reconsidered and supplied a new statutory explanation.

sections.title: Murphy explains why the first mandate permits a new agency judgment
sections.cue: Why had the first victory not entitled management to approval?
paragraphs: Justice Murphy’s opinion reaffirmed Chenery I: a reviewing court must evaluate the grounds the agency actually invoked, stated clearly enough for judicial scrutiny. The first order failed because its asserted judicial authorities did not support it. That conclusion did not resolve the policy judgment the statute committed to the SEC, and it did not create a vested right to management’s requested distribution.

The Commission remained responsible for determining whether the proposed amendment met the Act’s requirements. On remand it could, and had to, exercise that delegated function afresh. A court could not invent an administrative rationale for the old order, but the agency could supply its own informed rationale in a new decision. Here the court had an actual agency explanation to review, preserving rather than abandoning the allocation of decision-making authority underlying Chenery I.

sources.pinpoint: Rule and Holding; Reasoning 1–2; 332 U.S. at 196–201

sections.title: The lack of an earlier rule does not require approval of this application
sections.cue: When can an agency develop a principle through adjudication?
paragraphs: Management objected that no preexisting general rule prohibited the purchases. The Court answered that the SEC nevertheless had to approve or deny the particular amendment before it. An agency cannot knowingly approve a transaction inconsistent with the governing statute simply because it did not anticipate the precise problem in a prospective rule.

The Court recognized the advantages of general rules announced for future application. But a novel problem may need immediate resolution, the agency may lack sufficient experience to frame an enduring rule, or the circumstances may be too specialized and variable for one uniform prescription. Choosing between rulemaking and case-by-case development therefore lies primarily within the agency’s informed discretion. That principle does not excuse failure to follow rulemaking procedures that Congress separately requires.

Application to already completed purchases did have a retroactive effect. The Court weighed the loss of management’s expected gains against the injury to the statutory design that approval would permit. It likened a first administrative adjudication to a first-impression judicial decision that applies a newly articulated principle to earlier conduct. Retroactivity was a matter requiring evaluation, not automatic invalidation. The holding addressed this adjudicative application; it did not authorize retroactive legislative rules or every conceivable retrospective sanction.

sections.title: The SEC explains the conflicts created by management’s position
sections.cue: Why could good-faith purchases still threaten the statute’s purposes?
paragraphs: The renewed explanation focused on institutional incentives. Management could influence operating policies, accounting, disclosure, dividends, the timing and terms of reorganization proposals, and communications with the SEC. In a voluntary reorganization it represented shareholders, proposed and amended plans, and learned how the Commission was likely to respond. Its choices could affect both the market price of old securities and the allocation of new ones.

At the same time, a personal purchasing program gave management an interest in buying cheaply, securing favorable conversion terms, and preserving or increasing control. Those interests could conflict with its responsibility to investors as a whole. The Commission tied the conflict to statutory requirements of fair treatment and equitable voting-power distribution.

The Commission did not withdraw its acceptance of management’s personal good faith. It reasoned that divided incentives could affect conduct without conscious dishonesty, and attempts to investigate motives transaction by transaction could be costly, difficult, and inconclusive. A protective standard could therefore address the danger without proof of fraud in each purchase. The Supreme Court accepted that as an administrative judgment under the statute, not a newly discovered common-law breach.

The facts were uncontested, management acknowledged seeking the investment advantages and voting position produced by reorganization, and the SEC connected its concerns to those facts. The Court found a rational statutory foundation, substantial evidentiary support, and no plain abuse of discretion. It declined to replace the Commission’s authorized policy judgment with its own view of the wiser policy.

sections.title: The renewed order stands, while Jackson objects to retroactive prohibition
sections.cue: What did the judgment sustain and what did the dissent dispute?
paragraphs: On June 23, 1947, the Supreme Court reversed the Court of Appeals and sustained the renewed denial of the amendment. Management did not obtain parity conversion into new common shares under that application. The Court did not direct approval or order another explanatory remand. Justice Burton concurred only in the result, without explanation; the notation does not establish agreement with every part of Murphy’s rationale. Chief Justice Vinson and Justice Douglas did not participate.

Justice Jackson and Justice Frankfurter announced their disagreement with the June decision, and Jackson’s explanatory dissent, joined by Frankfurter, was filed October 6. Jackson regarded the result as abandonment of the protection supplied by Chenery I. The conduct, record, statute, and economic deprivation had not changed; in his view the SEC had repackaged the same unsupported result as expertise.

He emphasized lawful acquisition without an announced prohibition and the loss of ordinary appreciation in exchange for a limited recovery. General reorganization authority, he thought, did not supply an ascertainable rule authorizing that deprivation. Administrative experience deserved consideration within legal bounds, not as a replacement for law defining the bounds. He also questioned reliance on accumulated expertise for a problem described as newly encountered.

Above all, Jackson objected to announcing a prohibition after the transaction and applying it to the same parties whose conduct had previously been lawful. Fair notice, restraints on retroactive lawmaking, and meaningful judicial review controlled his analysis. His description of the decision as without law was the dissent’s critique; the majority found both statutory authority and adequate explanation. The two Chenery proceedings thus end differently because the agency grounds changed. The casebook’s subsequent Wyman-Gordon discussion is a later comparison, not another holding or stage of this dispute.

sources.pinpoint: Judgment; Separate Opinions; Notes; 332 U.S. at 209–18
